title: Equivariant learning of a transferable three-dimensional classical density functional
abstract: Liquids exhibit collective behavior that depends sensitively on thermodynamic conditions, interfaces and confinement, yet predicting each new state commonly requires a separate atomistic simulation. Classical density functional theory offers a reusable variational description, but its central excess free-energy functional is generally unknown, and learned approximations have largely remained restricted to planar or lower-dimensional settings. Here we show that this functional can be learned directly from fully three-dimensional equilibrium density fields while preserving spatial symmetry and variational consistency, without free-energy or chemical-potential labels. A single learned functional transfers across temperatures, system sizes and statistical ensembles, and recovers structure factors, the equation of state, liquid--vapor coexistence and interfacial broadening, none of which are used as training targets. Applied to complex three-dimensional geometries, it predicts the non-monotonic force associated with formation and rupture of a solvent-depleted bridge between colloids and adsorption in an interconnected gyroid pore. These results demonstrate that equilibrium density data can be converted into a transferable thermodynamic generator connecting microscopic liquid structure to response, phase behavior and collective phenomena.
summary: This work presents an equivariant machine learning framework to learn the excess free-energy functional for classical fluids directly from equilibrium density data. By enforcing local chemical potential balance, the model achieves remarkable transferability, accurately predicting macroscopic properties like phase behavior and interparticle forces in complex 3D environments without needing explicit labels for these targets.
main_problem: The central challenge is developing a transferable, three-dimensional classical density functional theory (cDFT) that can predict complex thermodynamic and structural properties from equilibrium density fields.
main_result: The authors successfully learned the excess free-energy functional using only density data, enabling predictions of structure factors, equation of state, phase coexistence, and even non-monotonic forces in confined geometries.
method: They introduced an equivariant learning framework (Equi-cDFT) that enforces local chemical potential balance ($\mu_{	ext{loc}, g} = 0$) to train the functional without requiring explicit free-energy or chemical-potential labels.
model_or_system: The theory applies to classical fluids, modeled using Lennard-Jones interactions, and is tested in various geometries including bulk fluid, colloid suspensions, and porous materials like gyroid structures.
key_observables: Structure factor $S(k)$, equation of state ($P(ho, T)$), liquid–vapor coexistence curves, one-body direct correlation function ($c^{(1)}_g$), and effective forces ($\langle F angle_D$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), density ($ho$), system size (e.g., $L=20\sigma$ for colloids), and external potential parameters.
main_assumptions: The method relies on enforcing the local chemical-potential balance condition ($\mu_{	ext{loc}, g} = 0$) as the primary learning signal, and it uses a finite receptive field approximation for transferability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the learned functional architecture using symmetry-adapted features, show recovered thermodynamic properties like $S(k)$ and isotherms across different states, and benchmark performance on colloid bridging forces and adsorption in porous media.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the Equi-cDFT framework by enforcing local chemical potential balance. It then derives key observables (like $c^{(1)}_g$ and $c^{(2)}$) via functional differentiation. The results are benchmarked across homogeneous fluids to recover EOS/phase behavior, followed by applications to complex systems like colloid bridging and adsorption in porous media.
why_interesting: While focused on classical liquids, the rigorous application of deep learning principles (equivariance, local constraints) to derive fundamental thermodynamic potentials is highly relevant for developing predictive models in quantum many-body physics where exact functionals are unknown.

Local neighborhoods of the three-dimensional density field are encoded using cubic- symmetry-adapted features and processed by a shared neural readout. Summing the local contributions produces an extensive excess free-energy functional, whose derivative gives the one-body direct correlation field. Here g labels a density-grid point, χg is its finite spherical environment, R ∈Oh denotes a rotation or reflection of the cubic lattice, Bg is the resulting symmetry- adapted feature vector and T is the temperature.
